lesson.title: Twelve Colonies, One Table: The First Continental Congress
lesson.summary: In the fall of 1774, delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia to coordinate a response to the Intolerable Acts, taking the first real step toward acting as a unified body.
lesson.body:
The Intolerable Acts convinced colonial leaders that Massachusetts could not be left to face Britain alone, since a Parliament willing to strip one colony's charter might do the same to any of them. In response, colonies chose delegates to meet in a general congress and coordinate a common strategy. This gathering, later called the First Continental Congress, convened in Philadelphia on September 5, 1774, and met at Carpenter's Hall, a guild meeting house chosen partly because the Pennsylvania State House was in use by the colonial assembly.

Fifty six delegates attended, representing twelve of the thirteen colonies. Georgia, distracted by conflicts with Native American nations on its frontier and dependent on royal support for its defense, sent no delegates. Even so, the range of colonies represented, from Massachusetts and Virginia to South Carolina, made this the broadest gathering of colonial leaders yet assembled in North America. Prominent delegates included Samuel Adams and John Adams of Massachusetts, Patrick Henry and George Washington of Virginia, and John Jay of New York. Peyton Randolph of Virginia was chosen as the Congress's president.

The delegates debated how far to go in resisting British policy. A moderate plan proposed by Joseph Galloway of Pennsylvania, which would have created an American legislature under continued British authority, was narrowly rejected. Instead, delegates from Massachusetts and Virginia pushed the body toward firmer action, and the Congress ultimately adopted the Continental Association, a coordinated boycott of British goods that also banned the export of colonial goods to Britain if grievances were not addressed by a set date. Local committees of observation and safety sprang up in towns across the colonies to enforce the boycott, giving ordinary colonists a direct role in the resistance movement for the first time.

The Congress also drafted a formal petition to King George III, known as the Declaration and Resolves, laying out colonial grievances and asking for the repeal of the Intolerable Acts and other objectionable laws while still professing loyalty to the crown. This was not yet a call for independence. Most delegates still hoped that a united, firm colonial response would persuade Parliament to change course and negotiate.

Before adjourning on October 26, 1774, the delegates agreed to reconvene the following May if their grievances remained unresolved. That single decision proved consequential, because when war broke out at Lexington and Concord in April 1775, the colonies already had a plan in place to meet again as a unified body, which they did as the Second Continental Congress just weeks later.

Massachusetts, still under military governor Thomas Gage and effectively stripped of its charter, treated the Congress as vital proof that its cause was shared well beyond New England, from the tobacco planters of Virginia to the merchants of South Carolina. That sense of shared danger, more than any single grievance, was what made twelve otherwise fiercely independent colonial legislatures willing to coordinate their response for the first time.
